content: Diseases that mimic the clinical presentation of cryptococcal meningitis, such as viral, bacterial, or tuberculous meningitis, should always be considered in the differential diagnosis. When clinically indicated, particularly in cases of culture-positive relapse despite adherence to fluconazole therapy, fluconazole susceptibility testing should be performed at a national reference laboratory. For individuals presenting with a relapse of cryptococcal meningitis, the following steps are recommended: 1. Initiate or reinitiate induction antifungal therapy as per established guidelines. 2. Address elevated intracranial pressure through therapeutic lumbar punctures. 3. Reinforce adherence to antifungal treatment regimens. 4. If antiretroviral therapy (ART) has not yet been initiated, it is recommended to start ART after 4–6 weeks of optimal antifungal therapy. 5. Consider fluconazole susceptibility testing if available. Cryptococcal disease is a significant opportunistic infection among individuals with advanced HIV, contributing substantially to morbidity and mortality. The disease primarily arises from the reactivation of latent infections in immunocompromised individuals, such as those living with HIV, often months to years after initial exposure. Cryptococcal meningitis is the most common manifestation, accounting for up to 90% of HIV-associated cryptococcal disease cases. In 2014, it was estimated to cause 223,100 cases and 181,100 deaths globally among people living with HIV, representing 15% of all HIV-related deaths. Other less common presentations of cryptococcal disease include pulmonary involvement, as well as skin, lymph node, and bone infections. Cryptococcal disease is rare in children with HIV, even in regions with a high burden of the disease among adults. Mortality from cryptococcal meningitis remains disproportionately high in low-income countries, with an estimated one-year mortality rate of 70% compared to 20–30% in high-income countries. Contributing factors include delays in diagnosis due to limited access to lumbar punctures and rapid diagnostic assays, as well as the high cost and limited availability of recommended antifungal drugs and intensive care. Additional challenges include the inability to monitor and manage treatment-limiting toxicities, complications of raised intracranial pressure, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) associated with cryptococcal meningitis and ART. A public health approach emphasizing prevention, early diagnosis, and improved treatment is critical to reducing the incidence and mortality of cryptococcal meningitis, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. New guidelines have been developed following a 2021 randomized trial supporting the use of a single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B-containing regimen as part of induction therapy. These guidelines aim to provide updated, evidence-based recommendations for treating adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV who have cryptococcal disease. They are intended for HIV program managers, policymakers, healthcare professionals, and individuals living with HIV. Key principles guiding these recommendations include: A public health approach to scaling up antiretroviral drug use along the continuum of HIV prevention, care, and treatment. Rapid ART initiation regardless of CD4 cell count or immune status as a critical strategy to reduce opportunistic infections. Early diagnosis and prompt initiation of optimal antifungal therapy to improve survival and clinical outcomes in HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. Prompt referral for HIV testing and care following a diagnosis of cryptococcal disease to facilitate ART uptake. Deferring ART initiation by 4–6 weeks in confirmed cryptococcal meningitis cases to reduce the risk of central nervous system IRIS and excess mortality. Implementation of these recommendations should be tailored to local contexts, including HIV epidemiology, the burden of cryptococcal disease, and the prevalence of comorbidities. All individuals living with HIV who test positive for cryptococcal antigen should undergo a thorough evaluation for meningitis symptoms and, if feasible, a lumbar puncture to exclude cryptococcal meningitis. Rapid cryptococcal antigen assays in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), serum, plasma, or whole blood are preferred due to their superior diagnostic accuracy compared to the India ink test and their reduced dependence on provider skill. Lateral flow assays are particularly advantageous due to their rapid turnaround time, cost-effectiveness, minimal training requirements, and higher sensitivity. However, these assays do not replace the need for lumbar punctures and CSF examination where feasible, as controlling intracranial pressure is critical for survival. In settings with limited access to lumbar punctures or where contraindications exist, such as coagulopathy or suspected space-occupying lesions, rapid serum, plasma, or whole-blood cryptococcal antigen assays are recommended. If these assays are unavailable, prompt referral for further investigation and treatment is advised. Screening for cryptococcal antigenemia is the optimal approach for guiding resource allocation in public health and is recommended for individuals aged 10 years or older with advanced HIV disease. Fluconazole primary prophylaxis remains an option in settings where cryptococcal antigen screening is unavailable. ART initiation among individuals with cryptococcal meningitis should be deferred by 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment to mitigate the risk of increased mortality. Preemptive antifungal therapy is recommended for individuals testing positive for cryptococcal antigen to prevent invasive disease. This involves fluconazole therapy followed by consolidation and maintenance phases. Cryptococcal antigen screening followed by preemptive therapy is preferred over primary prophylaxis due to cost considerations, the risk of antifungal resistance, and concerns about fetal safety in women of childbearing age without adequate contraception.
